::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Determining the best possible substitution for an integrand](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1116827/determining-the-best-possible-substitution-for-an-integrand), asked by [user208567](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/208567/user208567) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2015-01-23; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> What substitution is best used to calculate  $$\int \frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x^2 -1}}dx$$
:::

The quadratic form suggests $x = \sec\theta$.  But rationalizing first gives
$$\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x^2-1}} = \frac{\sqrt{x^2-1}-1}{x^2}$$
Now substituting $x=\sec\theta$ yields (after some algebra)
$$\int\frac{\sqrt{x^2-1}-1}{x^2}\,dx = \int(\sec\theta - \cos\theta - \sin\theta)\,d\theta$$
